request.system: You are a quantitative researcher in a small research lab. The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday, plus pre-registered products of some of them with market states. The base rung is trained on each sector's return over the next 4 weeks relative to the average of the 9, and each week's score is a weighted average of its scores of the current and recent weeks, so the book trades less. Your job is to propose ONE new feature with an economic mechanism that could improve the cross-sectional ranking beyond these six. Features are computed only from past weekly prices, so they cannot use the future. You never trade and you never see raw prices. Always answer with one JSON object.

response: {"mechanism": "A sector-specific volatility shock (recent idiosyncratic volatility running well above its own longer-run level) signals an elevated flow of sector-specific news and disagreement. Cross-sectional evidence (Ang et al. on idiosyncratic volatility, and the volatility-term-structure/vol-shock literature) shows that assets whose vol has just spiked relative to their own history tend to underperform over the following weeks: risk-budgeted and vol-targeting investors cut exposure mechanically, uncertainty-averse investors demand a discount, and vol spikes cluster around negative earnings/regulatory news whose drift is incomplete. Conversely, sectors whose vol has quietly compressed relative to their own norm tend to attract inflows and drift up. Expected sign: negative (high vol-shock ratio predicts relative underperformance over the next 4 weeks).", "rationale": "VOL13 is a cross-sectional LEVEL of volatility and is 0.96 correlated with BETA52, so it mostly re-expresses the permanent beta ordering (utilities/staples low, tech/energy high). A within-sector ratio of short-horizon to long-horizon volatility is level-free: a utility can have a high ratio and a tech ETF a low one, so it reorders sectors in a way almost orthogonal to beta and VOL13. Computing it on returns relative to the S&P 500 removes common market-wide vol swings (which cannot reorder sectors anyway) and isolates sector-specific shocks. It is also distinct from DD13/REV1/momentum since it is sign-agnostic: a sector that jumped up on news gets the same shock flag as one that dropped.", "feature_idea": "Weekly log relative return r_t = diff(1, log(ratio(close, spy))). Compute short vol s4 = rolling std over 4 weeks of r_t and long vol s26 = rolling std over 26 weeks of r_t. Feature = cs_z( ratio(s4, s26) ), i.e. a volatility-term-structure / vol-shock ratio, z-scored across the 9 sectors each Friday. DSL: {\"name\":\"IVOL_SHOCK_4_26\",\"expr\":{\"op\":\"cs_z\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"std\",\"n\":4,\"x\":{\"op\":\"diff\",\"n\":1,\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}}}}},\"b\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"std\",\"n\":26,\"x\":{\"op\":\"diff\",\"n\":1,\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}}}}}}}} (12 nodes). The model should learn a negative loading; an optional variant scales it by VIX via mul_state at the root if vol shocks matter more in high-vol regimes."}

The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday, plus pre-registered products of some of them with market states. The base rung is trained on each sector's return over the next 4 weeks relative to the average of the 9, and each week's score is a weighted average of its scores of the current and recent weeks, so the book trades less. response: {"mechanism": "Anchoring on the 52-week high (George & Hwang 2004): investors use the one-year high as a reference point and are reluctant to bid a sector above it even when fundamentals justify it, so good news is impounded slowly and sectors trading near their 52-week relative high keep outperforming over the following weeks, while sectors far below their high (where the anchor is stale and bad news is also under-reacted to) keep lagging. Measuring the high on the sector-to-SPY relative price strips out the common market swing, so the anchor is about sector-specific standing rather than whether the whole market made a new high. Expected sign: positive (closer to the 52-week relative high -> higher relative return over the next 4 weeks).", "rationale": "DD13 is a drawdown from a 13-week high on the absolute close, so it is dominated by the last quarter's market move and is strongly tied to REV1 and MOM26_1 (corr 0.40 and 0.49); a one-year relative-price anchor is a different horizon and a level (position inside the past year's range) rather than a return. MOM26_1 and MOM52_4 are point-to-point returns, which can be identical for a sector that climbed steadily to a fresh high and one that spiked and then collapsed; the nearness-to-high term distinguishes these paths. Because it is built on close/SPY it is also roughly beta-neutral, unlike VOL13/BETA52 which are near-collinear (0.96) and would otherwise absorb any market-driven high/low effect.", "feature_idea": "REL_HIGH52: compute the relative price R_t = close_t / spy_t each week; take its rolling 52-week maximum; feature = log(R_t / max_{52w} R). Then cs_z across the 9 sectors. In the DSL: {\"name\":\"REL_HIGH52\",\"expr\":{\"op\":\"cs_z\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"log\",\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}},\"b\":{\"op\":\"rolling\",\"stat\":\"max\",\"n\":52,\"x\":{\"op\":\"ratio\",\"a\":{\"input\":\"close\"},\"b\":{\"input\":\"spy\"}}}}}}} (10 nodes). Values are <= 0; sectors at a new relative high score 0 and get the top z-score. Optional variant if overlap with REV1 is a concern: replace the numerator with lag n=1 of the relative price so the last week's move is excluded."}

You are a quantitative researcher in a small research lab. The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday. Your job is to propose ONE new feature with an economic mechanism that could improve the cross-sectional ranking beyond these six. Features are computed only from past weekly prices, so they cannot use the future. You never trade and you never see raw prices. Always answer with one JSON object.

response: {"veto": true, "reasons": "Three concrete problems. (1) Sign contradiction: the stated mechanism (anchoring, George & Hwang) predicts a positive relation between nearness to the 52-week relative high and subsequent relative return, but the realised rank IC is negative (mean -0.02, t = -1.41). The Sharpe uplift therefore cannot be coming from the hypothesised mechanism; whatever the model is doing with this feature, it is not 'sectors near their relative high keep outperforming'. A feature whose standalone sign contradicts its own economic story is exactly the profile of a fitted artefact rather than a priced effect. (2) Redundancy with the momentum block: correlations of 0.755 with MOM26_1 and 0.72 with MOM52_4 (plus 0.51 with DD13) in a 9-name cross-section mean the feature is mostly a path-smoothed restatement of momentum. The only genuinely new content is the small residual 'path' component, and the most plausible way a weakly negative-IC feature produces a +0.16 Sharpe uplift when added to two highly collinear momentum features is that the model is using it as a differencing term against MOM26_1/MOM52_4 with a sign that is not pinned down by theory. Such near-collinear spread terms have unstable loadings across windows and are a classic source of in-sample uplift that evaporates out of sample. (3) The evidence base is thin: the base rung itself has a negative net Sharpe (-0.49 to -0.33), so the uplift is a smaller loss, and with the IC t-stat below 1.5 in absolute value and the sign inverted, P(uplift>0)=0.94 on a bootstrap of a single in-sample walk-forward is not enough to overcome the mechanism mismatch. If the author wants to pursue this, they should re-submit with the mechanism rewritten to match the observed negative sign (and defend why a 1-4 week horizon should show reversal rather than anchoring continuation), or orthogonalise the feature against MOM26_1/MOM52_4 before z-scoring so the incremental path term is tested directly. As submitted, I veto."}

request.system: You are a risk officer reviewing a proposed trading feature. Answer in JSON.

response: {"veto": false, "concern": null, "notes": "Construction is coherent: log of (close/spy) divided by its own trailing 52-period max is a bounded (<=0) distance-from-relative-high measure, cross-sectionally standardised; the SPY normalisation cancels any index-level drift so the signal is purely relative. This is a known momentum-style proxy with no obvious artefact or lookahead (rolling max includes the current bar, so no division-by-zero or future leakage). Sector tilt risk is the generic one for any momentum feature and is already bounded by the residual-beta check. Minor note for the team, not a veto: the name implies 52 weeks but n=52 on daily bars is ~2.5 months; confirm the bar frequency matches the intent."}

response: {"mechanism": "Momentum that is built from many small, consistent relative gains continues more reliably than momentum produced by one or two large jumps (the 'frog-in-the-pan' / information-discreteness effect): gradual, low-salience outperformance is under-reacted to by investors, whereas a single large move is quickly priced and more prone to reversal. Across sectors, a sector whose 26-week outperformance of the S&P 500 is large relative to the week-to-week dispersion of that outperformance (a high t-statistic of relative return) should keep outperforming over the next 4 weeks, while a sector with the same raw momentum but a choppy, jump-driven path should not. The hedge in the book makes the SPY-relative formulation the natural one: it isolates the sector-specific trend from market direction and from beta.", "rationale": "MOM26_1 is the raw relative return and VOL13 is the sector's own total volatility (and VOL13 is 0.96 correlated with BETA52, so it is mostly a beta proxy). Neither measures the smoothness of the sector's relative trend: the ratio of relative momentum to idiosyncratic (SPY-relative) weekly volatility is a nonlinear combination the linear base rung cannot form, and the denominator uses tracking volatility versus SPY rather than total volatility, which is almost uncorrelated with the existing VOL13/BETA52 pair. It also differs from the two failed candidates: IVOL_SHOCK used only the vol ratio with no sign, and REL_HIGH52 used distance from the relative high; this feature is a signed trend-quality (information ratio) measure over 26 weeks skipping the last week.", "feature_idea": "Let r(t) = diff(1, log(close/spy)) be the weekly log return relative to the S&P 500. Denominator: lag(1, rolling(std, 26, r)) = tracking volatility of the same 26 weekly relative returns. Feature = cs_z( ratio(numerator, denominator) ), i.e. the cross-sectionally z-scored 26-week relative-return t-statistic (relative information ratio). A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday, plus pre-registered products of some of them with market states. The base rung is trained on each sector's return over the next 4 weeks relative to the average of the 9, and each week's score is a weighted average of its scores of the current and recent weeks, so the book trades less. Your job is to propose ONE new feature with an economic mechanism that could improve the cross-sectional ranking beyond these six. Features are computed only from past weekly prices, so they cannot use the future. You never trade and you never see raw prices. Always answer with one JSON object.

Feature idea: {"feature_idea":"Compute the relative log price r(t) = log(close(t)/spy(t)). Take the 52-week relative return ending 52 weeks ago: x(t) = r(t-52) - r(t-104), i.e. diff with n=52 applied to lag n=52 of log(ratio(close, spy)). Cross-sectionally z-score it each Friday: cs_z(diff(52, lag(52, log(ratio(close,spy))))). The model is expected to assign a negative weight (high year-2 relative return -> lower expected relative return). Name: REL_LTREV_104_52. Optionally a mul_state with BEAR24 could be tested later, since reversal is often stronger after market drawdowns, but the plain cs_z version is the proposal.","mechanism":"Long-horizon relative reversal. Sectors that strongly outperformed the market one to two years ago attract capital, capacity expansion and analyst over-extrapolation; as supply responds and valuations normalise, their relative returns over the following months tend to lag (DeBondt–Thaler long-term reversal, sector capital-cycle effects). Conversely sectors that lagged the index in year -2 have had time for capacity to shrink and expectations to reset, so their relative returns over the next 4 weeks should be modestly positive. The effect is slow-moving, which suits the score smoothing and low turnover of the book, and it is a different horizon regime from the 1-week and 6-12 month windows the base model already sees.","rationale":"All six base features look back at most 52 weeks (MOM52_4 covers roughly t-52 to t-4, MOM26_1 t-26 to t-1, DD13/VOL13 13 weeks, REV1 one week, BETA52 a covariance not a return). No feature measures relative performance in the window t-104 to t-52, so year-2 reversal is unspanned; it should be only mildly (negatively) correlated with the momentum features because its window does not overlap theirs. It also differs from the earlier candidates: REL_HIGH52 (distance from 52w relative high), IVOL_SHOCK (volatility ratio) and REL_IR26 (risk-adjusted 26w momentum) are all within-52-week signals."}

response: {"mechanism": "Upside-tail (lottery) effect at the sector level. A sector that has printed an unusually large single-week outperformance versus the S&P 500 within the last quarter attracts attention-driven, return-chasing flows (retail and trend followers piling into the 'hot' sector ETF), which pushes its price above fundamentals; as that flow fades over the following weeks the sector underperforms the cross-section. This is the Bali-Cakici-Whitelaw MAX effect and the skewness-preference result of Boyer-Mitton-Vorkink, applied to relative (market-stripped) weekly returns so that market-wide jump weeks do not contaminate it. Expected sign: negative (high MAX -> lower relative 4-week return), i.e. a reversal of the extreme week, in contrast to continuation of the smooth trend captured by momentum.", "rationale": "VOL13 measures symmetric dispersion of total returns and is 0.96 correlated with BETA52, so the base rung effectively has one 'riskiness' dimension; it says nothing about the asymmetry or jumpiness of the recent return path. REV1 only looks at the last week, so an extreme week 3-10 weeks ago is invisible to it, while MOM26_1 sums over 26 weeks and treats a gradual 8% gain identically to a single 8% jump (the frog-in-the-pan distinction). DD13 captures the downside path only. Dividing the 13-week maximum relative weekly return by the 26-week standard deviation of relative weekly returns makes the feature a scale-free upper-tail/skew measure, so it is not just volatility in disguise. It also differs from the earlier candidates: IVOL_SHOCK_4_26 compared recent to longer-run dispersion (symmetric), REL_HIGH52 was a level-based drawdown, REL_IR26 a smooth trend-per-risk, and REL_LTREV a 1-2 year reversal.", "feature_idea": "Let r(t) = diff(1, log(close/spy)) be the weekly relative log return. Compute MAX13 = rolling max over 13 weeks of r, and SD26 = rolling std over 26 weeks of r. Feature = cs_z( MAX13 / SD26 ), name REL_MAX13_SKEW. The model learns the sign; expected coefficient negative (sectors with a recent outsized up-week relative to SPY, normalised by their own relative-return scale, tend to give back part of it over the next 4 weeks). Optional variant for a later trial: scale by VIX via mul_state, since lottery overpricing is stronger when attention/volatility is high, but the plain cs_z version should be tested first."}

response: {"mechanism": "Sector rotations unfold gradually: when a sector's relative performance versus the S&P 500 accelerates (its last 13 weeks of relative return beat its prior 13 weeks), investors underreact to the change in trend, so the recent leg tends to continue over the following weeks; a decelerating sector (strong older half, weak recent half) is a fading theme that tends to keep slipping. This 'momentum acceleration' or trend-curvature effect (second difference of the relative price path) is documented in equities and sector/industry portfolios and has a horizon that matches the 4-week target.", "rationale": "MOM26_1 and MOM52_4 are level momentum: they sum the two halves of the look-back and give a 13-week gain the same weight whether it occurred recently or six months ago, so two sectors with identical 26-week momentum but opposite curvature get the same score. REV1 only looks at one week, DD13 measures distance from a high (not the shape of the path), and VOL13/BETA52 are risk levels (and nearly collinear with each other). None of the rejected candidates used a second difference: the IR, 52-week-high, long-term reversal and max/skew ideas were all level or dispersion statistics. Scaling by relative volatility keeps the feature from being just a proxy for VOL13 in high-vol sectors.", "feature_idea": "REL_ACCEL_13_13: let r = log(close/spy) be the sector's relative log price. Compute recent half-year leg R_recent = r(t-1) - r(t-14) (diff of n=13 on lag-1 to skip the last week and avoid overlapping REV1) and earlier leg R_prior = r(t-14) - r(t-27) (lag 14 of the same 13-week diff). Acceleration = R_recent - R_prior. Divide by the 26-week rolling std of weekly relative log returns (diff n=1 of r) so the curvature is in risk units, then cs_z across the 9 sectors. In DSL terms: cs_z( ratio( a = diff(n=13, lag(n=1, r)) minus-via-diff: equivalently diff(n=13, diff(n=13, lag(n=1, r))) which equals r(t-1) - 2 r(t-14) + r(t-27), b = rolling std n=26 of diff(n=1, r) ) ). Optionally a mul_state with VIX at the root could test whether acceleration matters more in high-uncertainty regimes, but the plain cs_z version is the primary proposal."}

You are a quantitative researcher in a small research lab. The lab studies a weekly strategy that ranks 9 anonymised US sector ETFs (codes A1 to A9) after each Friday close; the top 2 are bought and the bottom 2 sold the next Monday, with a market hedge. A model (the base rung) already ranks them on six features: MOM26_1 (26-week momentum skipping the last week), MOM52_4 (12-1 month momentum), REV1 (last week's return), VOL13 (13-week daily volatility), DD13 (drawdown from the 13-week high) and BETA52 (52-week market beta), each z-scored across the 9 sectors every Friday. response: {"veto": false, "reasons": "Attacked on three fronts, none produces a disqualifying defect. Redundancy: max |corr| 0.047 with the six features, and the construction (4w/26w std ratio) is genuinely orthogonal to VOL13 (a level, not a ratio) and to REV1 (signed, not magnitude); it is not a relabelling of an existing input. Plausibility: a short-run vol spike relative to the sector's own 26w norm is a recognised regime-shift/uncertainty signal with a defensible mechanism (sectors in transient stress tend to be mispriced relative to their long-run risk, and the cross-sectional z puts it on a relative basis), and the feature uses only past closes. Overfitting: the honest weaknesses are (a) a 4-observation std is a very noisy estimator, essentially |recent returns| scaled; (b) rank_ic_t=1.85 is not significant after 7 candidates in this run; (c) a Sharpe uplift of 0.79 against an IC of 0.03 is disproportionate and suggests much of the gain comes from how the refit model reweights rather than from strong standalone ranking power. However, the walk-forward is out-of-sample by construction, bootstrap P(uplift>0)=1.0 is far above the 0.80 gate, drawdown is within tolerance (+0.16), and the leakage/warm-up checks are clean. These concerns justify monitoring (expect the realised uplift to shrink toward the IC-implied level, and consider a 6-8 week short window to reduce estimator noise in a future revision) but they are not a concrete reason to veto."}
